historical_timeline.summary: Scarlet fever in Vienna; two weeks in bed.
Violent fever at The Hague with weeks of weakness.
Smallpox at Olmütz; blind for nine days.
Illness described as cholera during an epidemic in Vienna.
His father's letter describing his illness in Vienna with fever, daily colic and violent vomiting.
Repeated requests to Michael Puchberg for loans.
La clemenza di Tito first performed in Prague.
Took to his bed with swelling of the hands and feet and vomiting.
Died in Vienna; the death record gives "hitzigen Friesel Fieber".
Blessed at St. Stephen's and buried in a general grave at St. Marx.

claims.statement: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg on January 27, 1756, the son of Leopold Mozart, a musician in the service of the Archbishop of Salzburg. Of the seven children of his parents' marriage only two survived: his sister Maria Anna, born July 30, 1751, and Wolfgang.
In Vienna in late 1762, on the family's second journey, an attack of scarlet fever kept him in bed for a fortnight.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A childhood febrile illness named by his biographer; the modern record does not re-diagnose it.

claims.statement: At The Hague in the autumn of 1765, after his sister's dangerous illness, he was seized with a violent attack of fever that reduced him to extreme weakness for several weeks; he kept writing on a board laid across his bed.

In 1767 the family fled a smallpox outbreak in Vienna to Olmütz, but he and then his sister caught smallpox there; the family was taken in by Count Leopold Anton von Podstatzky, Dean of Olmütz, and his illness was so severe that he lay blind for nine days and had to protect his eyes for several weeks afterwards.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented smallpox in childhood; the modern record notes it as past history.

claims.statement: In the spring of 1783 he fell ill with an illness his biographer calls cholera, during an epidemic in Vienna.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The eighteenth-century term may mean an acute gastroenteritis rather than modern cholera; it is not re-diagnosed.

claims.statement: In a letter to his daughter dated September 14, 1784, Leopold Mozart wrote that his son had been very ill in Vienna: he had become overheated at Paisiello's new opera and had gone out into the open air to find the servant who had his overcoat, and this "brought on rheumatic fever, which without careful attention might have turned to typhus." He quoted his son's letter: "I have had raging colic every day for a fortnight at the same hour, accompanied by violent vomiting," and that his doctor, Sigmund Barisani, visited him almost daily.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic episode: a febrile illness in Vienna at 28 with abdominal pain and vomiting, which his father called rheumatic fever. The eighteenth-century term does not establish a modern diagnosis. His own letter describing the illness is lost; the account survives in his father's letter, quoted from an English translation.

claims.statement: In 1784, up to the time of the episode, he lived at Graben 29 in Vienna.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Places him in Vienna at the start of the synthetic episode.

source_links.locator: residence list: Graben 29, January to October 1784

claims.statement: From October 1784 to April 1787 he lived at Domgasse 5 in Vienna.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index visit; places him in Vienna for the rest of the synthetic episode.

claims.statement: His mother died in Paris on July 3, 1778, while traveling with him, after an illness of some weeks during which she was bled; the cause is not recorded in the cited source.

He was appointed imperial chamber musician on December 7, 1787, with a salary of 800 gulden a year, but despite constant work he was in financial difficulty; from 1788 he repeatedly asked his fellow Freemason Michael Puchberg, a merchant, for loans, and at his death he owed Puchberg about a thousand florins. In April 1789 he also borrowed a hundred florins from Franz Hofdemel.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode. The record makes no claim that poverty caused his death.

source_links.locator: Vol. 2, letters to Puchberg; Hofdemel loan

claims.statement: He was in Prague in September 1791 for the coronation opera La clemenza di Tito, first performed there on September 6, 1791, and returned to Vienna.

Around November 20, 1791, he became seriously ill and took to his bed in his apartment in the Rauhensteingasse in Vienna. According to the accounts of his widow and his sister-in-law Sophie Haibel, his hands and feet began to swell, he had partial paralysis and violent vomiting, and he remained conscious through a fortnight in bed; his physician Dr. Closset called Dr. Sallaba, chief physician at the hospital, into consultation on November 28. He died at about one o'clock in the morning on December 5, 1791, aged 35. A letter from Prague of December 12 reported that "dropsy set in" and that the swelling of his body after death led to suspicions of poisoning.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode. The documented hallmark of the final illness is severe swelling; the cause of death is not documented by any modern standard.

source_links.locator: fell ill around November 20; died December 5
died December 5, 1791; severe edema in eyewitness accounts

claims.statement: The official record of his death gives the cause as "hitzigen Friesel Fieber" (hitziges Frieselfieber, an acute fever with a miliary eruption).
claims.clinical_interpretation: The eighteenth-century term describes fever with a rash and does not identify a modern disease.

claims.statement: His body was blessed at St. Stephen's Cathedral and buried in St. Marx cemetery outside the city, not in a mass grave but in a general, simple grave that was open to all social classes regardless of rank; no stone marked it, and its exact place is unknown.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The common grave was the ordinary burial of the time, not a pauper's burial; the roster's framing is not used.

source_links.locator: blessing and transfer to St. Marx

Vol. 3, no stone; resting place unknown

claims.statement: A 2009 study of the official Vienna death register for November 1791 to January 1792 and the same months of the years before and after found that deaths from edema were markedly increased among younger men in the weeks around his death, a minor epidemic that may have begun in the military hospital; the authors concluded that their analysis is consistent with his last illness being a streptococcal infection leading to an acute nephritic syndrome from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, with scarlet fever less likely.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation of the final illness (after the episode). The synthetic modern episode uses post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis because the evidence makes it a reasonable teaching diagnosis, not because it settles his real cause of death.

claims.statement: One author argues that he had frequent attacks of tonsillitis throughout his life and that in 1784 he developed a post-streptococcal Schönlein-Henoch syndrome.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation of his recurrent sore throats and the 1784 illness; used only as context for a modern post-streptococcal episode.

claims.statement: The same author proposes that the 1784 illness caused chronic glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney failure, that the fatal illness was Schönlein-Henoch purpura with death from cerebral hemorrhage and bronchopneumonia, and that bloodletting may have contributed to his death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation of the final illness; not adopted. Other authors disagree.

claims.statement: Many other causes of his final illness have been proposed, including kidney failure and trichinosis (argued in a 2001 review titled "What killed Mozart?"), and none has been established.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cause of death is not documented; these are retrospective interpretations.

claims.statement: In his last weeks he told his wife that he believed he had been poisoned, and rumors of poisoning circulated after his death, including a later accusation against Antonio Salieri. His nineteenth-century biographer calls the accusation a calumny, rebutted at the time by Carpani and Neukomm; no evidence supports poisoning.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The poisoning legend is unsupported and is recorded only so that it can be marked as such. The modern record does not use it.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care and nephrology for a 28-year-old composer and pianist with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: recognizing the acute nephritic syndrome (edema, cola-colored urine, hypertension, a rising creatinine, and red cell casts) two to three weeks after a sore throat; confirming a recent group A streptococcal infection and a low C3 with a normal C4; telling it apart from IgA nephropathy and IgA vasculitis, lupus, C3 glomerulopathy, and acute rheumatic fever, with the 2015 revised Jones criteria and an echocardiogram for the joint pains; outpatient supportive care with salt and fluid restriction, a loop diuretic, and blood pressure thresholds; antibiotics for the infection; avoiding NSAIDs; knowing when a kidney biopsy is needed; and following C3, creatinine, proteinuria, and hematuria until they recover. A sick visit for a cold teaches when not to test for strep, and the difference between synpharyngitic hematuria and a post-streptococcal relapse. Built on the KDIGO 2021 glomerular diseases guideline, the AHA 2015 Jones criteria statement, the IDSA 2012 streptococcal pharyngitis guideline, and the CMID chronic kidney disease and hypertension monographs.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Mozart returns two days after his first visit, on the day of his nephrology consultation with Dr. Okonkwo-Brandt. Since starting furosemide each morning he has passed much more urine, and he has lost about a kilogram, but his eyelids are still puffy in the mornings and his ankles swell by evening. The urine is lighter but still brownish. The colicky abdominal pain and vomiting have stopped, the knee and ankle aches are easing, and he has had no fever. He has a mild headache in the mornings, with no change in vision, confusion, chest pain, or breathlessness lying flat. He is taking penicillin twice a day and has stopped ibuprofen. He is keeping salt low and drinking about a liter and a half a day.

assessment.assessment: A typical acute nephritic syndrome, with red cell casts, edema, hypertension, and a rise in creatinine, appearing after a latent period of two to three weeks. There is firm evidence of a recent group A streptococcal infection and a low C3 with a normal C4. That is the classic pattern, and it makes a kidney biopsy unnecessary now. IgA nephropathy usually causes dark urine within a day or two of an infection, not weeks later, and does not lower C3. IgA vasculitis would usually bring purpura. Lupus would usually lower C4 as well. ANCA vasculitis and anti-GBM disease would be expected to run a more aggressive course with a normal C3. Ibuprofen may have added a little to the rise in creatinine. The creatinine is still rising, but he is passing more urine, his potassium is acceptable, and he has no pulmonary edema or hypertensive emergency, so outpatient care is safe with close review. The antibiotics clear the infection but do not change the course of the nephritis

assessment.display: Joint pains after streptococcal infection: acute rheumatic fever considered
assessment.assessment: In a low-risk population the 2015 revised Jones criteria need two major manifestations, or one major and two minor, with evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection. He has polyarthralgia, one minor manifestation. His fever never reached 38.5 °C, and his ESR and CRP are below the minor thresholds of 60 mm/h and 3.0 mg/dL. There is no arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, or nodules. The PR interval is normal, and Doppler echocardiography shows no carditis. He has no major manifestation, so the criteria are not met. Rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis seldom occur together. No secondary prophylaxis is needed
